question: When current G is not certified by absence observations, what can repeated imperfect detection actually rule out and how does probabilistic decision error depend on effort?

design.truth: original full G=A&B&M per candidate world, unchanged
design.sites: all grid nodes of each original landscape
design.observation: binary detections on k independent visits per site; detection probability p conditional on G=1, false positives fixed zero
design.non_detections: Likelihood (1-p)^k if G=1 and no detection; 1 if G=0 and no detection; any detection has zero likelihood for G=0
design.replicate_generation: exact analytical per-site likelihoods and exact dynamic programming for target-sign posterior; do not simulate unseeded pseudo-replicates
design.weights: one explicitly hypothetical uniform prior per DISTINCT A/B/M mask triple, not parameter-world labels, not an estimated ecological prior
design.decision: MAP target sign only if posterior mass >=0.95; otherwise abstain; report exact expected decisive-and-correct, decisive-and-wrong, abstention across observation patterns under each truth
design.computational: evaluate exhaustive detection bitmaps when small enough; otherwise exact DP by grouping distinct G masks and target signs, no truncation; fail closed on state explosion
design.baseline: under 0<p<1 and finite k, all candidate worlds with G superset of detections retain positive likelihood. Thus repeated non-detection never logically proves absence; separate logical identifiability from Bayesian posterior decision.
design.no_effect_claim: No natural species detection probabilities or causal inference; report model assumptions.

checks: all original 768 worlds and 12 systems unchanged
same target signs as prior M-release baseline121/129
no detection with p<1 cannot logically rule out occupied G
higher visit count changes probabilistic risk but not deterministic logical impossibility
report denominators and avoid parameter-label multiplicity as prior
